results.title: Theoretical Error Analysis of Entropy Approximation for Gaussian Mixture
results.content: # Theoretical Error Analysis of Entropy Approximation for Gaussian Mixture. More precisely, we prove the upper and lower bounds of the approximation error, which imply that the error is controlled by the ratios of the distances between the means to the sum of the variances of each (Gaussian) component of the Gaussian mixture, and the error converges to zero as the ratios tend to infinity (Definition 4.1 and Theorem 4.2). Consequently, our result guarantees that the approximate entropy works effectively, especially in situations involving neural network models like BNNs. Furthermore, we show the approximation error bound in the form of a probabilistic inequality (Corollary 4.3), justifying the intuition as mentioned above. We also provide the upper bounds for the partial derivatives of the error with respect to parameters (Theorem 4.4), which ensure that the derivatives of the approximate entropy used in back propagation in machine learning are also close enough to the true ones (when the ratios are large enough).

results.title: PAC-Bayesian Generalisation Error Bounds for Gaussian ...
results.content: ## PAC-Bayesian Generalisation Error Bounds for Gaussian Process Classification. ***Matthias Seeger***; 3(Oct):233-269, 2002. ### Abstract. Approximate Bayesian Gaussian process (GP) classification techniques are powerful non-parametric learning methods, similar in appearance and performance to support vector machines. Based on simple probabilistic models, they render interpretable results and can be embedded in Bayesian frameworks for model selection, feature selection, etc. In this paper, by applying the PAC-Bayesian theorem of McAllester (1999a), we prove distribution-free generalisation error bounds for a wide range of approximate Bayesian GP classification techniques. We also provide a new and much simplified proof for this powerful theorem, making use of the concept of convex duality which is a backbone of many machine learning techniques. We instantiate and test our bounds for two particular GPC techniques, including a recent sparse method which circumvents the unfavourable scaling of standard GP algorithms. As is shown in experiments on a real-world task, the bounds can be very tight for moderate training sample sizes. To the best of our knowledge, these results provide the tightest known distribution-free error bounds for approximate Bayesian GPC methods, giving a strong learning-theoretical justification for the use of these techniques.

results.title: Nyström Approximation in Gaussian Processes - Lukas Schneider
results.content: Nyström Approximation in Gaussian Processes - Lukas Schneider This website uses cookies to ensure you get the best experience on our website. Nyström Approximation in Gaussian Processes An intuitive introduction to the Nyström approximation in Gaussian Processes. Gaussian Processes (GPs) are a powerful Bayesian machine learning method. A problem, however, is that when inferring the value of a new data point (i.e. making a prediction with the GP), the kernel matrix K∈R n×n, where n is the number of training points, needs to be inverted. The inversion of a n×n matrix is a O(n 3) operation and therefore infeasible for large data sets. This inversion can be sped up by the matrix inversion lemma to a O(q 3) operation, where q is the rank of the matrix K (i.e. q≤n). We can use this lemma (besides the straighforward application if r a n k(K)<n) to speed up the GP inference by approximating K with a matrix K~ that is as similar to K as possible but with (much) smaller rank (similarity is measured with some matrix norm). To construct a good approximation) (optimal w.r.t. the Frobenius norm) with rank q, we need the q leading eigenvalues and eigenvectors of K. We therefore resort to approximating the eigenvalues and -vectors using the Nyström method. As this can be done in O(q 2 n), we can significantly speed up GP inference for a small value of q. (Of course, the smaller we choose q, the worse our approximation will be). Now, what do we actually need to do to compute the approximate kernel matrix? First, we select a sample of q<n elements from the training set. The approximate kernel is then computed as K~=[K 11 K 21]K 11−1[K 11 K 21 T] and can as such be used in the GP predictive equations by replacing the kernel matrix K=K(X,X) for the training points X (The kernels involving the test-points X⋆ are left untouched). This post is meant to give you an introduction to the Nyström approximation to help you understand the related literature. There, you can also find the concrete equations to approximate the eigenvalues and -vectors and how to use these to construct the approximate kernel.
